### Chapter 1: Setting Up Your Environment {.unnumbered}



#### Exercise 1

Both routes produce the same matrix, but only one of them needs a check
afterwards. `merge()` aligns two `xts` objects on their indices and pads any
date that one side lacks, so the assertion that nothing was padded is a
separate step. Binding the long tables first and crossing once leaves nothing
to align: a single `as_xts_pm()` call sees every date and every asset at once,
and a missing cell would be padded and announced by the coercion itself.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
MM <- as_xts_pm(sim_money_market_monthly, date, class, return)
wide_route <- merge(R, MM)
stopifnot(ncol(wide_route) == 21L, nrow(wide_route) == 372L, !anyNA(wide_route))

long_route <- dplyr::bind_rows(sim_class_returns_monthly, sim_money_market_monthly) |>
  as_xts_pm(date, class, return)
stopifnot(identical(colnames(wide_route), colnames(long_route)),
          identical(zoo::coredata(wide_route), zoo::coredata(long_route)))
c(columns = ncol(long_route), rows = nrow(long_route), missing = sum(is.na(long_route)))
#> columns    rows missing 
#>      21     372       0
```
:::


#### Exercise 2

Dropping the early `JP_equity` rows leaves one column short by the number of
months removed. `complete.obs` discards those months for every series;
`pairwise.complete.obs` keeps them for every pair that has them. A pairwise
matrix is not guaranteed to be positive definite, which is why the smallest
eigenvalue is worth reading. `PortfolioAnalytics` uses the pairwise estimate
for a variance objective.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
trimmed <- sim_class_returns_monthly |>
  dplyr::filter(!(class == "JP_equity" & tidypm::model_year(date) <= 3L))
R_trim <- suppressWarnings(as_xts_pm(trimmed, date, class, return))
R_trim <- R_trim[, colnames(R)]                  # restore the column order by name

range(colSums(!is.na(R_trim)))
#> [1] 336 372
S_complete <- stats::cov(R_trim, use = "complete.obs")
S_pairwise <- stats::cov(R_trim, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
differ   <- abs(S_complete - S_pairwise) > 1e-12
jp_cells <- outer(colnames(R) == "JP_equity", colnames(R) == "JP_equity", "|")
min_eig  <- min(eigen(S_pairwise, symmetric = TRUE)$values)
stopifnot(all((!differ) == jp_cells))            # the agreeing cells are exactly JP_equity's
c(entries_differing = sum(differ), entries_total = length(differ),
  jp_entries_differing = sum(differ & jp_cells), smallest_eigenvalue = min_eig)
#>    entries_differing        entries_total jp_entries_differing 
#>       225.0000000000       256.0000000000         0.0000000000 
#>  smallest_eigenvalue 
#>         0.0000008627
```
:::


225 of the 256 entries differ, and the
31 that agree are exactly the `JP_equity` row and column:
both estimators use the same 336 months there,
while for every other pair `complete.obs` discards
36 months that the series never lacked
and the pairwise estimate keeps them. The pairwise matrix
is positive definite here, with a
smallest eigenvalue of 8.6e-07; that is a property of
this gap, not a guarantee.

```{.r .cell-code}
#>  2 add.objective_v2                  add.objective                  TRUE  
#>  3 constrained_objective_v1          constrained_objective          TRUE  
#>  4 constrained_objective_v2          constrained_objective          TRUE  
#>  5 constraint_v1                     constraint                     TRUE  
#>  6 constraint_v2                     constraint                     TRUE  
#>  7 optimize.portfolio.rebalancing_v1 optimize.portfolio.rebalancing TRUE  
#>  8 optimize.portfolio_v1             optimize.portfolio             TRUE  
#>  9 optimize.portfolio_v2             optimize.portfolio             TRUE  
#> 10 random_portfolios_v1              random_portfolios              TRUE  
#> 11 random_portfolios_v2              random_portfolios              TRUE
```

:::


13 of the 14 shims have an
unsuffixed counterpart; the exception is
`update_constraint_v1tov2()`, which exists only to
translate a constraint object written against the first interface into the
current one. Its name records that the constraint object itself changed shape
between the two interfaces, which is why code written against one does not run
against the other.


### Chapter 2: Notation and Data {.unnumbered}



#### Exercise 1

The hedge is the subtraction of @eq-02-hedge, applied series by series with the
exchange rate of the series' own region. Building the result as one data frame,
one row per series, keeps a bond from being paired with another region's
currency.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
fx <- sim_fx_monthly
foreign <- setdiff(colnames(R), grep("^(US|GLOBAL)_", colnames(R), value = TRUE))

hedge_table <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(foreign, function(s) {
  region <- sub("_.*$", "", s)
  f <- fx[fx$region == region, ]
  stopifnot(all(f$date == as.Date(zoo::index(R))))
  u <- as.numeric(R[, s])
  tibble::tibble(series = s, kind = sub("^[^_]+_", "", s),
                 unhedged = ann_vol(u), hedged = ann_vol(u - f$fx_return),
                 removed = 1 - stats::var(u - f$fx_return) / stats::var(u),
                 currency = ann_vol(f$fx_return),
                 local_with_fx = stats::cor(u - f$fx_return, f$fx_return))
}))

by_kind <- hedge_table |>
  dplyr::group_by(kind) |>
  dplyr::summarise(dplyr::across(c(unhedged, hedged, removed, currency), mean),
                   .groups = "drop")
by_kind |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(-kind, ~ round(.x, 3)))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   kind       unhedged hedged removed currency
#>   <chr>         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 credit        0.123  0.062   0.743    0.098
#> 2 equity        0.192  0.186   0.053    0.098
#> 3 government    0.102  0.038   0.853    0.098

removed <- setNames(by_kind$removed, by_kind$kind)
hedged  <- setNames(by_kind$hedged, by_kind$kind)
jp      <- hedge_table[hedge_table$series == "JP_equity", ]
stopifnot(all(removed[c("government", "credit")] > 0.5), removed[["equity"]] < 0.2,
          jp$local_with_fx < 0, jp$hedged > jp$unhedged)
```
:::


Hedging removes on average
85% of a foreign government
bond's variance and 74% of a
foreign credit class's, and
5% of a foreign equity market's. A
bond's local return is a few percent a year of yield and curve movement, a
hedged volatility of 3.8% for the
government classes, so the currency's swings of
10% a year dominate the dollar
return. An equity market's local volatility,
19% on average, is already
1.9 times the
currency's, and in Japan the local market tends to rise when the yen
falls, a correlation of -0.39, so the two partly
cancel before any hedge is applied and hedging raises the volatility of
`JP_equity` from 19.6% to
21.2%. Currency is therefore a property of the
asset rather than of the country, and @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application
develops the point.

#### Exercise 2


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ids <- sim_assets$asset_id[sim_assets$asset_class == "commodity"]
stopifnot(length(ids) == 8L)

rebuilt_weekly <- sim_asset_returns_weekly |>
  dplyr::filter(asset %in% ids) |>
  dplyr::group_by(date) |>
  dplyr::summarise(return = mean(return), .groups = "drop")

shipped_weekly <- sim_class_returns_weekly |>
  dplyr::filter(class == "GLOBAL_commodity")
stopifnot(all(rebuilt_weekly$date == shipped_weekly$date))

rebuilt_monthly <- rebuilt_weekly |>
  dplyr::mutate(month = lubridate::floor_date(date, "month")) |>
  dplyr::group_by(month) |>
  dplyr::summarise(return = prod(1 + return) - 1, .groups = "drop")

shipped_monthly <- sim_class_returns_monthly |>
  dplyr::filter(class == "GLOBAL_commodity") |>
  dplyr::mutate(month = lubridate::floor_date(date, "month"))
stopifnot(all(rebuilt_monthly$month == shipped_monthly$month))

gaps <- c(weekly_gap  = max(abs(rebuilt_weekly$return - shipped_weekly$return)),
          monthly_gap = max(abs(rebuilt_monthly$return - shipped_monthly$return)))
stopifnot(gaps < 1e-12)
gaps
#>            weekly_gap           monthly_gap 
#> 0.0000000000000004025 0.0000000000000004927
```
:::


Both gaps are at machine precision. The commodity class is exactly the equally
weighted mean of its eight instruments, rebalanced weekly, and the monthly
series is exactly that weekly portfolio compounded within each month. The same
holds for every government and credit class; only the equity classes are
weighted by anything other than $1/n$.

#### Exercise 3


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ids <- sim_assets$asset_id[sim_assets$asset_class == "equity" & sim_assets$region == "US"]

caps <- sim_marketcap_weekly |>
  dplyr::filter(asset %in% ids) |>
  dplyr::arrange(asset, date) |>
  dplyr::group_by(asset) |>
  dplyr::mutate(cap_prev = dplyr::lag(market_cap)) |>   # previous week, never this one
  dplyr::ungroup()

weekly <- sim_asset_returns_weekly |>
  dplyr::filter(asset %in% ids) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(caps, by = c("date", "asset")) |>
  dplyr::group_by(date) |>
  dplyr::mutate(half = ifelse(cap_prev >= stats::median(cap_prev), "larger", "smaller"))

two_ways <- weekly |>
  dplyr::summarise(equal = mean(return),
                   value = sum(cap_prev * return) / sum(cap_prev),
                   larger  = mean(return[half == "larger"]),    # equally weighted
                   smaller = mean(return[half == "smaller"]),   # within each half
                   .groups = "drop")

shipped <- sim_class_returns_weekly |> dplyr::filter(class == "US_equity")
stopifnot(nrow(two_ways) == nrow(shipped), all(two_ways$date == shipped$date))

ex3 <- c(value_vs_shipped = max(abs(two_ways$value - shipped$return)),
         ann_ret_value    = ann_ret(two_ways$value, p = 52),
         ann_ret_equal    = ann_ret(two_ways$equal, p = 52),
         correlation      = stats::cor(two_ways$value, two_ways$equal),
         ann_ret_larger   = ann_ret(two_ways$larger, p = 52),
         ann_ret_smaller  = ann_ret(two_ways$smaller, p = 52))
stopifnot(ex3[["value_vs_shipped"]] < 1e-12,
          ex3[["ann_ret_equal"]] > ex3[["ann_ret_value"]],
          ex3[["ann_ret_smaller"]] > ex3[["ann_ret_larger"]])
round(ex3, 4)
#> value_vs_shipped    ann_ret_value    ann_ret_equal      correlation 
#>           0.0000           0.1298           0.1512           0.9492 
#>   ann_ret_larger  ann_ret_smaller 
#>           0.1306           0.1697
```
:::


The value-weighted rebuild reproduces the shipped series to machine precision,
which confirms both the weighting and the one-week lag. The equally weighted
version earns
2.1
percentage points a year more and correlates with the shipped series at
0.95. The gap is a small-cap tilt: sorted
each week on the previous week's capitalization, the smaller half of the names
earned 17.0% a year and the
larger half 13.1%, and an equal
weighting holds far more of the small ones than their capitalization warrants.
A benchmark should be value-weighted, because that is the portfolio every
investor could hold simultaneously; an equal weighting is a strategy, and
@sec-21-equity-sleeve-implementation treats it as one.


### Chapter 3: Return, Risk, and the Investor's Problem {.unnumbered}



#### Exercise 1

The count is the same computation on a different grid. Weekly returns are the
model's native frequency and the monthly returns are compounded from them, so
the two panels describe the same path.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
Rw  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_weekly, date, class, return)
# The weekly bill starts one week before the returns do, so it is matched by
# date rather than subtracted by position.
rfw <- sim_riskfree_weekly$return[match(zoo::index(Rw), sim_riskfree_weekly$date)]
stopifnot(!anyNA(rfw), ncol(Rw) == 16L)
Rew <- Rw - rfw

dominance <- function(X, scale) {
  m <- tibble::tibble(asset = colnames(X),
                      mu    = as.numeric(colMeans(X)) * scale,
                      sigma = as.numeric(apply(X, 2, stats::sd)) * sqrt(scale))
  m$dominated_by <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(m)), function(i)
    sum(m$mu >= m$mu[i] & m$sigma <= m$sigma[i]) - 1L, integer(1))
  m$kind <- ifelse(m$dominated_by > 0L, "dominated", "efficient")
  m
}
both <- dplyr::inner_join(dominance(Re, 12), dominance(Rew, 52),
                          by = "asset", suffix = c("_monthly", "_weekly")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(changed = kind_monthly != kind_weekly) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(mu_monthly))
both |>
  dplyr::transmute(asset,
                   mu_monthly = round(mu_monthly, 4), mu_weekly = round(mu_weekly, 4),
                   sigma_monthly = round(sigma_monthly, 4), sigma_weekly = round(sigma_weekly, 4),
                   kind_monthly, kind_weekly) |>
  as.data.frame()

#> 14 JP_credit            0.018     0.0185        0.112        0.117  dominated

c(changed = sum(both$changed))
#> changed

```
:::


No series changes status
between the two grids, although every moment moves. The property at stake is
the one @eq-03-annualize assumes: multiplying a mean by the number of periods
and a standard deviation by its square root is exact only when returns are
independent across periods and add rather than compound. Weekly returns
compound into monthly ones, so the monthly arithmetic mean carries the cross
terms of that product and the monthly variance carries the week-to-week
autocovariances that the weekly count sets to zero. The differences reach
0.19
percentage points on the means and
1.42
on the volatilities, the largest of them on
UK_equity, and a
series would have to sit within that margin of the boundary of
@eq-03-dominance to cross it. On this sample none does.

#### Exercise 2

Lo's correction and the direct calculation should agree where its assumptions
hold: returns that are stationary and aggregate by summation.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
lo_factor <- function(v, q) {
  rho <- stats::acf(as.numeric(v), lag.max = q - 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[-1]
  q / sqrt(q + 2 * sum((q - seq_len(q - 1)) * rho))
}
direct <- function(v, q) {
  agg <- if (q == 3) xts::apply.quarterly(v, function(z) prod(1 + z) - 1)
         else             xts::apply.yearly(v,    function(z) prod(1 + z) - 1)
  mean(agg) / stats::sd(agg)
}
cmp <- tibble::tibble(
  asset   = colnames(Re),
  monthly = apply(Re, 2, function(v) mean(v) / stats::sd(v)),
  lo_3    = monthly * apply(Re, 2, lo_factor, q = 3),
  direct_3  = vapply(colnames(Re), function(a) direct(Re[, a], 3),  numeric(1)),
  lo_12   = monthly * apply(Re, 2, lo_factor, q = 12),
  direct_12 = vapply(colnames(Re), function(a) direct(Re[, a], 12), numeric(1))
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(gap_3 = direct_3 - lo_3, gap_12 = direct_12 - lo_12) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(abs(gap_12)))
cmp |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(-asset, ~ round(.x, 3))) |> as.data.frame()

#>  8 CH_government      0.065 0.113    0.11  0.241     0.225 -0.004 -0.016
#>  9 JP_credit          0.046 0.073    0.077 0.141     0.155  0.005  0.015
#> 10 UK_government      0.06  0.106    0.101 0.219     0.205 -0.005 -0.014
#> 11 CH_equity          0.154 0.274    0.259 0.55      0.562 -0.016  0.013
#> 12 GLOBAL_commodity   0.068 0.112    0.115 0.222     0.23   0.003  0.007

# The annual gaps are the larger ones, and they sit on the series with the largest ratios.
gap_vs_level <- stats::cor(abs(cmp$gap_12), cmp$lo_12, method = "spearman")
stopifnot(max(abs(cmp$gap_3)) < max(abs(cmp$gap_12)), gap_vs_level > 0.5)
```

:::


At $q = 3$ the two agree to within
0.04 for every series. At $q = 12$ the
gaps reach 0.07, for two reasons that
are not failures of the formula. @eq-03-lo aggregates by summation, while the
direct calculation compounds, so the cross terms of @eq-03-compound enter the
annual series and not the formula; and the annual series has only
31 observations, so its Sharpe ratio
is itself estimated with a standard error of roughly
$1/\sqrt{31}$. The gaps are largest
on the series with the largest ratios,
`US_credit`, `US_equity`, `US_government` first, with a rank
correlation of 0.68 between the absolute gap and
the ratio: a given relative error in the annual standard deviation moves a
large ratio by more. Eleven estimated $\rho_k$ enter the correction as well,
and each carries its own sampling error.

#### Exercise 3

The subtraction is the same; the answer is not.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
fx <- sim_fx_monthly
hedge_stats <- function(series, region) {
  f <- fx$fx_return[fx$region == region]
  stopifnot(all(fx$date[fx$region == region] == zoo::index(R)))
  u <- as.numeric(R[, series]); loc <- u - f
  c(unhedged = stats::sd(u) * sqrt(12), hedged = stats::sd(loc) * sqrt(12),
    removed = 1 - stats::sd(loc) / stats::sd(u), cov_local_fx = stats::cov(loc, f) * 12)
}
eq <- tibble::tibble(region = c("EU", "UK", "CH", "JP"), series = paste0(region, "_equity"))
jp <- hedge_stats("JP_equity", "JP")
stopifnot(jp[["hedged"]] > jp[["unhedged"]], jp[["cov_local_fx"]] < 0)   # the hedge adds volatility
round(t(mapply(hedge_stats, eq$series, eq$region)), 4)
#>           unhedged hedged removed cov_local_fx
#> EU_equity   0.2112 0.1922  0.0897      -0.0007
#> UK_equity   0.1773 0.1604  0.0954      -0.0013
#> CH_equity   0.1825 0.1793  0.0171      -0.0047
#> JP_equity   0.1960 0.2124 -0.0840      -0.0085
```
:::


Hedging `JP_equity` raises its volatility, from
19.6% to
21.2%. By
the decomposition $\operatorname{Var}(R^{\$}) = \operatorname{Var}(R^{\text{loc}})
+ \operatorname{Var}(f) + 2\operatorname{Cov}(R^{\text{loc}}, f)$, the hedge
removes the last two terms, and it can only add volatility when the covariance
is negative and large enough to outweigh the currency's own variance. That is
the case for Japan, where the covariance is
-0.0085 on an
annualized basis: the market rises when the yen falls, so the currency is a
hedge that the investor already holds, and a forward contract removes it. For
a government bond the local return is small and nearly uncorrelated with the
currency, so the currency's variance is most of the total and the hedge
removes most of the risk.

#### Exercise 4

The relaxed-budget volatility is monotone in $\gamma$, so the $\gamma$ that
reproduces a 60/40 volatility is a root.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
mu <- colMeans(Re); S <- stats::cov(Re)
p_vol <- function(w) sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w)) * sqrt(12)

eq_i <- grepl("_equity$", colnames(Re)); gv_i <- grepl("_government$", colnames(Re))
w_6040 <- setNames(rep(0, ncol(Re)), colnames(Re))
w_6040[eq_i] <- 0.6 / sum(eq_i); w_6040[gv_i] <- 0.4 / sum(gv_i)
stopifnot(abs(sum(w_6040) - 1) < 1e-12)

relaxed_spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "weight_sum", min_sum = 0, max_sum = 1) |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")
w_relaxed <- function(gamma) {
  spec <- relaxed_spec |>
    add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
    add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "var", risk_aversion = gamma / 2)
  extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, spec, optimize_method = "ROI"))[colnames(Re)]
```

With both bounds active, the first-order condition is

```{.r .cell-code}
lambda  <- ifelse(at_cap,  lambda0 - Sw, 0)
```

The interval of @eq-27-constant is $(0, 2c_f)$, so the first three constants
lie inside it and the fourth outside. In the simulation the three inside beat
$N/T = 0.267$ and the one at $2.5\,c_f$ gives
0.119,
still below the sample
mean's risk; the positive part is why a constant outside the interval
does not do the damage the unclamped formula predicts,
because once $c/(T\hat{q})$ exceeds one the factor is held at zero rather
than turning negative. In the backtest the Sharpe ratio of the tangency rule
rises monotonically
with $c$, from 0.671 to
0.851: a larger constant shrinks
harder, more windows collapse onto minimum variance, and on this market
minimum variance is the better rule, so the Sharpe ratio rewards shrinkage
beyond the risk-minimizing constant. The two criteria disagree because the
theorem minimizes the risk of the mean while the backtest scores a long-only
rule against a rival that uses no mean.
